subject: Anthropology
title: Remote Sensing
description: A quick, practical guide to Remote Sensing.

hook.text: Hidden temples in Cambodian jungles were found not by machetes but by lasers shot from airplanes.

buildup.text: Remote sensing uses technology to find sites without digging — satellite images, aerial photos, and ground radar.

discovery.text: LiDAR strips away tree cover digitally, revealing ancient roads, buildings, and canals hidden for centuries.

twist.text: Ground-penetrating radar can map buried structures without moving a single stone. Archaeology is going non-invasive.

climax.text: Remote sensing is transforming archaeology. We can now find and study sites that would have taken decades to discover.

punchline.text: Technology sees what the jungle hides.

quiz.question: What does LiDAR do for archaeology?
options: It digitally removes vegetation to reveal hidden structures

details.summary: Remote sensing uses technologies like satellite imagery, aerial photography, LiDAR, and ground-penetrating radar to detect archaeological features without excavation. LiDAR has been particularly revolutionary, revealing entire hidden cities beneath forest canopy.
details.whyItMatters: Remote sensing allows archaeologists to discover and map sites without disturbing them. LiDAR's ability to see through vegetation has revealed that civilizations were far larger and more connected than previously believed.
takeaways: Remote sensing detects archaeological sites without excavation
LiDAR penetrates vegetation to reveal hidden structures beneath
These technologies have revolutionized our understanding of past civilizations

faq.question: How has LiDAR changed archaeology?
faq.answer: LiDAR fires laser pulses that penetrate forest canopy and map the ground surface beneath. It revealed vast hidden Maya cities, enormous Khmer urban networks around Angkor, and extensive pre-Columbian earthworks in the Amazon, transforming understanding of these civilizations.

faq.question: Can remote sensing replace excavation?
faq.answer: No. Remote sensing reveals patterns on and below the surface but cannot recover artifacts, analyze materials, or determine precise chronologies. It is a powerful complement to excavation — identifying where to dig and providing landscape-scale context.
